newsitem.title: COSTA RICA: Central America to go for broke with Clinton visit.
newsitem.headline: Central America to go for broke with Clinton visit.

text.p: Given a rare chance to meet a U.S. president on their own turf, Central American leaders will seek a free-trade agreement with President Bill Clinton and a reprieve for tens of thousands of immigrants facing deportation from the United States, officials say.
Clinton will hold a summit with his Central American counterparts in San Jose, Costa Rica, on Thursday, then venture into the tropical rain forest on Friday for a bit of ecotourism.

Clinton is set to meet with eight other heads of state in Costa Rica, the peaceful and relatively prosperous country on the isthmus that is sometimes called "the Switzerland of Central America." His first-ever Central American visit will come between stops in Mexico and Barbados.

The Central Americans will be placing a tall order during the summit. They want a free-trade agreement with the United States, their top export market, similar to what Mexico received with the North American Free Trade Agreement.
Moreover, the Central Americans as a group will ask for residency visas for tens of thousands of immigrants, mostly Guatemalans and Nicaraguans, who are stranded in the United States in legal limbo.

Most were war refugees never formally granted asylum but allowed to stay under vague guidelines. Central Americans will ask that the United States take them on for good, arguing that their fragile economies cannot handle a massive repatriation.
None of the Central American leaders is predicting a major breakthrough, though, in large part because while Clinton may support their cause, he faces a sceptical Congress back home.
Signing free-trade agreements in Latin America and taking on more immigrants are highly unpopular on Capitol Hill.

"There are themes that the United States is very non-committal on ... such as the free-trade treaty," President Armando Calderon Sol of El Salvador told reporters. "A visit from President Clinton won't make sense if we can't speak frankly with him."

But for the most part the Central American countries are happy to receive Washington's attention at all after the years of neglect that followed a long period of U.S. involvement in the region's Cold War-era civil conflicts.

Former President Ronald Reagan made stopping communism in Central America a centrepiece of his foreign policy after a leftist guerrilla movement came to power in Nicaragua and others were threatening the governments of El Salvador and Guatemala in the 1980s.

"Central America was the subject of exteme attention, but negative, during the era of crisis and war," Gabriel Aguilera, Guatemala's deputy foreign minister told Reuters. "Now we'd like to have the same level of interest and support but on a positive level with Central America now at peace."

Indeed, the lesson Central Americans have learned over the past two decades is that there was plenty of U.S. money for guns but little for butter. The United States poured untold billions of dollars into the region during wartime in the 1980s but now hands out far less than $1 billion a year.

Presidents of the five Central American countries -- Guatemala, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Honduras and Costa Rica -- will be joined by the leaders of Panama and Belize, also on the isthmus, and the Caribbean island nation Dominican Republic.

Many of those countries are best known for war and poverty, but Costa Rica, by comparison a pillar of wealth and stability, is ideal for the regional summit. The last time a president visited Central America, George Bush went to Costa Rica in October of 1989.
